rca.judge_reason: The analysis names the 09:31 CI deployment of payments-api as the root cause. It treats the NullReferenceException as a code defect introduced by that release, which matches the ground truth's deployment correlation. It also correctly recommends a rollback.
rca.root_cause: A recent deployment to payments-api (MICROSOFT.APP/CONTAINERAPPS/WRITE by ci-deployer@contoso.example at 2026-10-11T09:31:12Z) introduced a code defect causing a System.NullReferenceException on the POST /v1/payments/capture endpoint, producing 500 responses and an 18.4% failure rate.

scenarios.title: Bad deploy throws NullReferenceException on capture

findings.title: Failed traces localized to downstream dependencies for orders-api
Latency dominated by downstream dependencies for orders-api

rca.judge_reason: The analysis names the orders SQL database dependency as the root cause, citing the 62.1% dependency failure rate localized by traces, and treats the API 500s and latency as downstream symptoms. That matches the ground truth's dependency_failure. It guesses saturation or blocking rather than a platform fault in the elastic pool, but the failing component and causal direction are correct.
rca.root_cause: The orders-api is failing because its downstream Azure SQL database (orders-sql.database.example) is unavailable or saturated. SQL connections are timing out during the post-login phase (SqlException code -2, 'Connection Timeout Expired'), causing a 62.1% dependency failure rate that propagates into HTTP 500 errors on the API's read and write endpoints.

scenarios.title: Azure SQL outage fails order reads and writes

findings.title: Azure Resource Health degraded for checkout-web

rca.judge_reason: The analysis identifies the platform-initiated Resource Health transition to Unavailable as the root cause, and treats the 503s as the resulting symptom. This matches the ground truth. Its recommendation to restart or deploy a new revision is a minor flaw. It also lists failover, so the root cause itself is right.
rca.root_cause: A platform-initiated availability event caused the checkout-web container app to transition from Available to Unavailable at 2026-10-11T03:07:44Z, resulting in a near-total service outage. The subsequent 96% request failure rate with GET /checkout returning 503 errors is the direct symptom of the app being unavailable at the platform level.

scenarios.title: Azure platform event takes checkout-web offline

rca.judge_reason: The analysis identifies memory exhaustion in ledger-api as the root cause, which matches the resource_exhaustion category, and it treats the latency and OOM errors as consequences. It does not name the specific non-evicting cache, but it suggests a possible leak and points to reviewing recent deployments. That covers the same underlying cause.
rca.root_cause: The ledger-api container app is experiencing memory exhaustion, with System.OutOfMemoryException being thrown and causing HTTP 500 failures on POST /v1/ledger/entries. Memory pressure is driving severe latency degradation (P95 4200ms, P99 7800ms) as the runtime spends excessive time in garbage collection and fails to service requests, producing the observed error spike.

scenarios.title: Memory leak drives ledger-api into GC thrash and OOM

findings.title: Failed traces localized to downstream dependencies for payments-api

rca.judge_reason: The analysis names the degraded external fraud-scoring partner as the root cause. It cites the 88% of request time spent in that call and does not blame payments-api or recommend scaling, which matches the ground truth's dependency_failure.
rca.root_cause: The payments-api latency degradation and 504 errors are caused by the downstream dependency fraud-score.partner.example. Traces for POST /v1/payments/authorize show 88% of the 3650ms end-to-end time is spent in this downstream call, and all 8 failed traces are localized to this dependency (HTTP code Canceled), surfacing as TaskCanceledException ('A task was canceled.') in application logs and 504 Gateway Timeout responses to clients.

scenarios.title: Third-party fraud scoring API slows to 3 seconds

rca.judge_reason: The ground truth says this was normal background noise with no root cause to name. The analysis does note the low 0.2% rate and that the service is healthy. But it never concludes the alert is noise. Instead it asserts a root cause: client-side timeouts and cancellations, possibly aggravated by tail latency. It also recommends remediation work, which is the false-alarm outcome the ground truth warns against.
rca.root_cause: The failures on notifications-api are client-side disconnections (HTTP 499) rather than server faults. 6 POST /v1/notifications/send requests returned 499, correlating with TaskCanceledException/HttpRequestException and the explicit exception message 'The client disconnected.' Clients closed the connection before the server completed the request, most likely due to client-side timeouts or cancellations.

scenarios.title: Exception-count alert flaps on normal background noise

rca.judge_reason: The analysis makes no claim about why identity-api is failing and states that the cause remains undetermined with zero confidence. It correctly attributes the blind spot to uniform 403 access denials on Log Analytics and Application Insights. It proposes no remediation for the incident itself, only restoring read access and re-running the investigation. This matches the expected behavior when there is no evidence.
rca.root_cause: The investigation could not be completed because the credentials (likely the investigation agents' managed identity or service principal) lack the required RBAC permissions to read telemetry. All four data-collection agents (Activity Log, logs, traces, metrics) failed with HTTP 403 InsufficientAccessError when querying Log Analytics workspace 'golden-workspace' and Application Insights 'golden-app-insights'. This is a tooling/access failure, not a confirmed fault in the identity-api container app itself.

scenarios.title: Real outage while the platform's telemetry access is revoked

findings.title: Failed traces localized to downstream dependencies for session-api
Latency dominated by downstream dependencies for session-api

rca.judge_reason: The analysis identifies the container app configuration write at 10:05:37Z as the root cause. It ties that write to the service pointing at the decommissioned Redis endpoint. It treats the Redis connection failures as a consequence, not an independent outage. This matches the ground truth.
rca.root_cause: A container app configuration change to session-api (MICROSOFT.APP/CONTAINERAPPS/WRITE at 2026-10-11T10:05:37Z) left the service pointing at a stale/decommissioned Redis endpoint (sessions-cache-old.redis.cache.windows.net:6380), which the app can no longer reach. The resulting StackExchange.Redis.RedisConnectionException (UnableToConnect) at a 100% dependency failure rate is driving the request failures and latency on session-api.

scenarios.title: Config change points session-api at a decommissioned Redis

rca.judge_reason: The analysis hedges among three candidates: a slow downstream dependency, resource saturation, or a regressing deployment. It does not commit to CPU exhaustion or the traffic surge, and it tells responders to check dependencies and deployments first. High request volume and saturation appear only as a contributing factor among several hypotheses.
rca.root_cause: The catalog-api container app is experiencing significant latency degradation, with P95 at 2600ms and P99 at 4100ms, while maintaining a 0.0% failure rate across 15,800 requests in the most recent minute. The absence of errors combined with elevated latency points to a performance bottleneck (likely a slow downstream dependency, resource saturation, or a recent performance-regressing deployment) rather than a hard failure.

rca.judge_reason: The analysis names the recent pricing-api deployment as the root cause of a performance regression and recommends rolling back, which matches the ground truth. It mentions dependency or resource saturation only as unconfirmed alternatives, without hedging away from the deploy as the chosen cause. It does not identify the specific regex mechanism, but naming the failing deploy is sufficient.
rca.root_cause: A recent container app deployment to pricing-api (MICROSOFT.APP/CONTAINERAPPS/WRITE at 2026-10-11T15:02:09Z by ci-deployer@contoso.example) introduced a performance regression, driving P95 latency to 2450ms and P99 to 3900ms with no corresponding increase in failure rate.

scenarios.title: Deploy ships a slow pricing rule and latency doubles

rca.judge_reason: The analysis identifies the deterministic FormatException that settlement-api's parser throws on the new partner amount format '1.234,56' as the cause of the 500s on the batch endpoint. It rules out infrastructure and dependency problems and recommends fixing the parser and reprocessing the failed batches. This matches the ground truth.
rca.root_cause: The settlement-api is throwing System.FormatException when parsing numeric input formatted with European/locale-specific conventions (e.g. '1.234,56' using comma as decimal separator and period as thousands separator) in the POST /v1/settlements/batch endpoint. The parsing logic almost certainly uses an invariant or en-US culture that cannot interpret this format, causing all affected batch requests to fail with HTTP 500.

scenarios.title: Partner batch with European number format crashes the parser

rca.judge_reason: Correctly identifies the in-process mechanism, an attempt to use an already-disposed SslStream from the client that fails before any downstream call. But it attributes this to a recently introduced code regression and recommends reviewing deployments. The ground truth says nothing was deployed and the cause is transient bad state from a network blip, fixed by a restart. The analysis misses the trigger and the restart remedy and contradicts 'nothing changed'.
rca.root_cause: The documents-api is throwing System.ObjectDisposedException ('Cannot access a disposed object. Object name: SslStream') on the GET /v1/documents/{id} endpoint, causing HTTP 500 responses. This pattern strongly indicates the application is accessing an already-disposed SslStream/HttpClient connection — most likely due to improper lifecycle management of an HttpClient (or its underlying socket/SSL stream) used to call a downstream HTTPS dependency, such as disposing a shared HttpClient, reusing a disposed connection, or a prematurely cancelled/closed SSL connection.

scenarios.title: Disposed storage client leaves documents-api stuck after a network blip

findings.title: Latency dominated by downstream dependencies for profile-api

rca.judge_reason: The analysis identifies the Redis profile cache's 33% failure rate as the root cause, with the fallback to backend reads producing the added latency. This matches the ground truth dependency failure. It adds a speculative point about resiliency configuration as a compounding factor, but its chosen primary cause is the cache.
rca.root_cause: The Redis dependency profile-cache.redis.cache.windows.net:6380 is experiencing a 33% failure rate, causing profile-api to fall back to slower downstream paths. This is the dominant driver of degraded latency for the GET /v1/profile/{id} operation, which spends 88% of its 1250ms end-to-end time in downstream calls.

scenarios.title: Redis cache degrades but profile-api falls back to SQL

rca.judge_reason: The analysis does not identify the traffic collapse caused by an upstream routing change as the root cause; it says no root cause was found. It mentions 'possibly reflecting reduced traffic' and a 'traffic drop' only as one possibility among several, alongside a transient condition and a misconfigured alert. It also leans toward checking the alert configuration before treating this as a real incident. That is hedging without choosing the true cause.
rca.root_cause: No root cause could be conclusively identified from the available findings. The only signal present is a metrics-agent performance analysis showing healthy metrics (P95 95ms, P99 160ms, 0.0% failure rate) over a low-volume sample of 37 requests in the most recent minute, which does not corroborate the Sev1-Error alert severity.
